title.en: The Gods of Gunung Agung: Raffles' Account of Balinese Religion
title.zh: 阿貢山諸神：拉弗爾斯所記巴釐宗教

texts.period: Balinese religious tradition as recorded by Raffles in 1815 (published 1817), from a Balinese informant

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), Appendix (CCVIII-CCXI), the religion of Bali

summary.en: Raffles' appendix records the Balinese pantheon from an intelligent native informant: Batara Guru is 'the highest object of worship below the divinity, Sang Yang Tunggal (the lord who is one)'; the great deities of the island are Dewa Gede Segara (deity of the sea), Dewa Gede Dalam (emblematical of death), Dewa Gede Bali Agung, and above all Dewa Gede Gunung Agung, 'to whom all the Rajas and people of Bali pay adoration'; images of gold, silver, bell-metal and iron stand in temples on Gunung Agung, Batu, Batur-hakul and Predung.
summary.zh: 拉弗爾斯附錄自一位聰慧之巴釐本地人記錄島上神譜：巴塔拉·古魯為『至上神（桑·揚·通加爾，唯一之主）以下最高之崇拜對象』；島上大神為海神德瓦·格德·塞加拉、象徵死亡之德瓦·格德·達蘭、德瓦·格德·巴釐·阿貢，以及至高之德瓦·格德·阿貢山神——『巴釐列王與人民皆敬拜之』；金、銀、銅、鐵所鑄神像供於阿貢山、巴圖、巴圖爾-哈庫爾與普勒東之廟中。

sensitivity.note: Early-nineteenth-century record of living Balinese religion; paraphrase respectfully.

narrative.en:
Raffles' appendix to the History of Java preserves the earliest full English account of Balinese religion, given to him by 'an intelligent Mahometan, a native of the island' — a syncretic reporter describing the Hindu-Balinese system from within its neighbourhood.

BEGINNING: THE ONE AND THE HIERARCHY. The account places Batara Guru as the highest object of worship below the divinity Sang Yang Tunggal — 'the lord who is one.' Beneath this apex the Balinese pantheon distributes the island's sacred geography: Dewa Gede Segara is the deity of the sea; Dewa Gede Dalam is emblematical of death, with a temple near the kraton of the Raja; Dewa Gede Bali Agung is the deity in whose temple the common people worship on particular days; and Dewa Gede Gunung Agung is a deity still more generally worshipped, 'to whom all the Rajas and people of Bali pay adoration.'

MIDDLE: THE MOUNTAINS OF THE GODS. Images of the deities — some of gold, some of silver, some of bell-metal, some of iron — are housed in temples and dedicated places on Gunung Agung, Gunung Batu, Gunung Batur-hakul and Gunung Predung; 'but it is Gunung Agung that is the famous place for them, and those figures are the objects of worship to all the princes of Bali.' The volcano is the throne-room of the island's religion, and the rajahs' worship centres on its summit.

END: THE RUBRIC OF FESTIVALS. The informant closes with the calendar of devotion: at a tama'tum (festival on a grand occasion) all the Rajas with families and subjects repair to Gunung Agung and invoke the deities, the Maperwita Brahmana (the learned Brahmins called Padinda) conducting the ceremonies; marriages are sanctified by being witnessed by the Brahmanas and all the deities invoked; on the new moon and the eighth and twenty-third of the month all the deities are worshipped and 'thousands of people are afterwards fed with their consecrated fragments,' the Padinda administering holy water which the people drink and bathe with. On the day of the new year the deities are worshipped, ablutions performed, offerings made; cloths and money are offered twice a year; and there is the fast of Nyuapid, lasting a day and a night, during which food and sleep must be abstained from.

FUNCTIONS. The record (1) fixes the vertical theology of Bali (the One, Batara Guru, the Gede deities, the mountain temples); (2) ties the volcano to kingship and popular worship alike; (3) documents the priestly administration (Padinda) and the feeding of thousands on consecrated fragments; and (4) supplies the early external witness to the cycle of festivals still centred on the Day of Silence.
narrative.zh: 拉弗爾斯《爪哇史》附錄保存了巴釐宗教最早之完整英文記錄，出自『一位聰慧之本地穆斯林』之手——以鄰居身分描述印度教-巴釐體系。開篇：等級神學——桑·揚·通加爾（唯一之主）之下，巴塔拉·古魯為最高崇拜對象；其下分掌島之聖地：海神德瓦·格德·塞加拉、死亡之象徵德瓦·格德·達蘭（廟近王宮）、德瓦·格德·巴釐·阿貢，及至高之德瓦·格德·阿貢山神——『巴釐列王與人民皆敬拜之』。中段：諸神之山——金、銀、銅、鐵神像供於阿貢山、巴圖山、巴圖爾-哈庫爾與普勒東之廟；『阿貢山為其名區，諸像即巴釐列王崇拜之對象』——火山即全島宗教之寶座廳。結尾：節慶儀注——大節之日，列王攜家眷與臣民登阿貢山呼喚諸神，由瑪珀維塔婆羅門（即帕丁達）主持；婚禮須經婆羅門與所呼諸神見證；朔日與每月初八、廿三，眾神受拜，『成千之人以受祝之祭餘果腹』，帕丁達施聖水令民飲之浴之；新年之日拜神、行浴、獻祭；布與錢一年兩獻；另有『尼烏阿皮德』齋戒——一晝夜間絕食禁眠。功能：立巴釐縱向神學、繫火山於王權與民祀、記載帕丁達祭司之執禮與食聖餘之眾、並為今日『靜默日』節俗提供最早之外部見證。

functions: Fixes the vertical theology of Bali: the One, Batara Guru, the Gede deities, the mountain temples
Ties the volcano Gunung Agung to both kingship and popular worship
Documents the Padinda priesthood and the feeding of thousands on consecrated fragments
Provides the early external witness to the festival cycle of the Day of Silence

The deity Dewa Gede Segara is the deity of the sea; Dewa Gede Dalam is emblematical of death; Dewa Gede Gunung Agung is a deity still more generally worshipped, and to him all the Rajas and people of Bali pay adoration.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), Appendix; not verbatim.

passages.text: Images are made of the deities, some of gold, some of silver, some of bell-metal, and some in iron, and dedicated in temples on Gunung Agung, Gunung Batu, Gunung Batur-hakul and Gunung Predung; but it is Gunung Agung that is the famous place for them, and those figures are the objects of worship to all the princes of Bali.

When there happens to be a festival on a grand occasion, all the Rajas with their families and subjects repair to Gunung Agung and invoke the deities, the Maperwita Brahmana being summoned to conduct the ceremonies. Marriages are sanctified by being witnessed by the Brahmanas and all the deities invoked; on the new moon and the eighth and twenty-third of the month all the deities are worshipped, thousands of people are afterwards fed with their consecrated fragments, and the Padinda administers holy water which they both drink and perform ablutions with.

title.en: The Fast of Nyuapid: Bali's Day of Silence
title.zh: 尼烏阿皮德齋戒：巴釐靜默日

texts.period: Balinese new-year fast recorded by Raffles (1817); observed annually to the present

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), Appendix, the fast of Nyuapid

summary.en: Raffles' informant closes the Balinese calendar with the fast of Nyuapid — 'which lasts a day and a night, during which time food and sleep must be abstained from,' held on the first or the fifteenth of the month. This is the early record of Nyepi, the Day of Silence with which the Balinese new year begins: the island shuts down, fires and lights are doused, and work stops, so that the demons sweeping over the island find it empty and pass on.
summary.zh: 拉弗爾斯之報告人以『尼烏阿皮德』齋戒收束巴釐曆法——『歷一晝夜，其間禁食禁眠』，行於每月之首或十五日。此即靜默日（Nyepi）之最早記錄——巴釐新年始於全島止息：熄火滅燈、停止勞作，使巡島之魔靈見島空無一人而過。

sensitivity.note: Living observance; the empty-island explanation is the folk rationale of the fast.

passages.text: There is also the fast of Nyuapid, which lasts a day and a night, during which time food and sleep must be abstained from; this fast must be held on the first or the fifteenth of the month. The Day of Silence begins the Balinese new year: the island goes dark and still — no fire, no light, no work, no travel — so that the demons who sweep over Bali at the year's turning find it empty and pass it by.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), Appendix; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Nyepi tradition; not verbatim.

title.en: The Wayang of the New Year: Offerings at All the Market-Places
title.zh: 新年之哇揚：各集市之供品

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), Appendix, the new-year wayang offerings

summary.en: In Raffles' Balinese rubric, 'when it is Idn'uik wayang, which means the new year wayangs, offerings are made and placed at all the market-places, but no worship takes place' — and at the annual festivals of tampak kilwon offerings are made on account of all the different animals. The shadow-plays of the new year receive their own offerings, at the markets rather than the temples.
summary.zh: 拉弗爾斯所錄巴釐儀注：『值伊德努伊克·哇揚（即新年哇揚）之期，須備供品置於各集市，但不舉行崇拜』；歲末『坦帕克·基爾旺』節，並為各類動物備供。新年皮影戲自有其供——供於市場而非廟宇。

sensitivity.note: Market-place offerings recorded 1817; read alongside the wayang tradition's sacred status.

passages.text: When it is Idn'uik wayang, which means the new year wayangs, offerings are made and placed at all the market-places, but no worship takes place; and at the annual festivals of tampak kilwon there are offerings made on account of all the different animals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), Appendix; not verbatim.

title.en: Sakalan and Nikalan: The Two Halves of Balinese Religion
title.zh: 薩卡蘭與尼卡蘭：巴釐宗教之二分

region.zh: 巴釐島（宗教職分之二分）

texts.period: Balinese religious division recorded by Raffles (1817)

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), Appendix, the two divisions of Balinese religion

summary.en: The religion of Bali, Raffles' informant explains, is divided into Sakalan and Nikalan: the first regards all worldly concerns — the orders of the prince, the laws of the land, the common affairs and transactions of life; the second comprehends all the duties and ceremonies of religion, 'the conducting of which is in the hands of the Maperwita, or learned Brahmins called Padinda.' Sacred and secular are one system with two offices.
summary.zh: 拉弗爾斯之報告人釋曰：巴釐宗教分為薩卡蘭與尼卡蘭：前者掌一切俗務——王者之命、國之法律、日常事務；後者總宗教之一切職責與儀典，『其主持之權在瑪珀維塔——即受學之婆羅門，名帕丁達』。聖俗一體，惟執掌有二。

sensitivity.note: Structural note on Balinese religious organization recorded 1817.

passages.text: The religion of Bali, as it exists on Bali, is divided into Sakalan and Nikalan. The first regards all worldly concerns, such as the orders of the prince, the laws of the land, and the common affairs and transactions of life; the second comprehends all the duties and ceremonies of religion, the conducting of which is in the hands of the Maperwita, or learned Brahmins called Padinda.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), Appendix; not verbatim.

title.en: Barong and Rangda: The Lion, the Widow and the Kris Dancers
title.zh: 巴龍與蘭達：獅、寡婦與持克里斯的舞者

texts.period: Balinese ritual drama; early twentieth-century documentation (Spies and de Zoete 1938) on older village foundations

source.work: The Barong and Rangda drama (Calonarang play) of Balinese village temples

summary.en: At the temple festival the shaggy lion-barong — kept in the temple shed as a village treasure — dances against Rangda the widow-witch, fangs and mane of white hair, whose leyak followers swarm at her call. Young men with kris dance the baris between them; at the climax Rangda's power enters them and they turn the daggers on their own breasts, which cannot pierce — the play ends not with victory but with the community's evidence that both powers must be kept inside the village boundary.
summary.zh: 廟節之時，毛蓬蓬的獅形巴龍——作為全村之寶供於廟棚——與寡婦巫蘭達對舞：蘭達利齒白髮如鬣，其黎雅克徒眾聞呼而至。持克里斯的青年舞於兩者之間；高潮處蘭達之力入其身，他們反將短刃刺向自己胸膛——卻刺之不入。戲不以勝負收場，而以『兩種力量都必須留在村界之內』的明證作結。

sensitivity.note: Living ritual drama; treat with respect; do not describe as spectacle without its protective function.

texts.canonical_translation: Based on the standard documentation of the Calonarang play; paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The Barong-Rangda drama is Bali's central living rite of the boundary between the village and the dangerous outside — performed at temple festivals in nearly every community, with the two faces of the myth carried by the same village.

BEGINNING: THE LION IN THE SHED. The barong is a shaggy lion-dragon mask worked in leather and mirror, kept in the temple's shed between performances and fed and honoured as a village treasure; it is the protective power of the community, led by comic followers, danced by two men inside the costume.

MIDDLE: THE WIDOW COMES. Rangda — the widow-witch whose legend goes back to Calon Arang of Girah — enters the square: fangs, pendulous breasts, and the mane of white hair; her followers, the leyak, swarm behind her, and she brings the sickness and madness that once plagued Airlangga's kingdom. The kris dancers of the village (the baris) dance against her; she casts her power at them, and at the climax the dancers turn their daggers on their own breasts in trance — the blades bending, unable to pierce.

END: THE BOUNDARY HELD. The play does not end in a victor: Rangda retreats toward the graveyard and the barong stands between; the trance is broken gently with incense and the dancers are led back to themselves. The village has tested its boundary — the destructive force was met, entered the young men's bodies even, and was returned outside the line. The drama is thus not a tale but an instrument: it maintains the edge where the community's protection stops and the wilderness of the leyak begins.

FUNCTIONS. The drama (1) maintains the village boundary against the leyak world; (2) transmits the Calon Arang legend as embodied memory; (3) manages possession safely inside ritual (the kris-on-breast climax under the priests' supervision); and (4) balances the village's two faces — the barong's nurture and Rangda's menace — as both necessary, both owned, both kept in the temple precinct. The performance's management is as carefully codified as its myth: the kris dancers are men chosen and prepared by the village, the trance is induced and released under the direction of the pemangku and the barong's handlers, and the blades that turn on the dancers' breasts are pressed flat, never driven — the danger is displayed and mastered in the same gesture. The two masks are owned, not opposed: villages keep both in the temple's sheds, feed and dress them on their days, and the drama's calendar follows the temple's odalan. The Rangda figure carries the Calon Arang legend's whole cargo — widowhood, grudge, plague, and the king's counter-plot — into dance, so that the historical narrative of the Pararaton lives as embodied memory in the square. Comparative mythologists read the pair as a boundary-instrument: the village's protective power and its projected menace, locked in a balance the community itself conducts.
narrative.zh: 巴龍-蘭達戲劇是巴釐『村界內外』核心活態儀式——幾乎各村廟節皆演，神話之兩面由同一村落承載。開篇：廟棚中的獅子——巴龍為皮革與鏡片所作之蓬鬆獅龍面具，演出間供奉於廟棚、受人餵養禮敬，是村社之護佑力，由二名舞者藏於道具之內，率丑角隨員起舞。中段：寡婦登場——其傳說上溯格拉鎮之加隆·阿朗——利齒、垂乳、白髮如鬣；黎雅克徒眾蜂擁其後，帶來昔年荼毒艾爾朗加國之病與瘋。村中持克利斯之青年（巴里）與之對舞；蘭達施力於其身，高潮處舞者入恍惚，反將短刃刺向己胸——刃彎而不入。結尾：戲不分勝負——蘭達退向墳場，巴龍立於其間；以香火輕撫喚醒恍惚者。村界經受考驗：毀滅之力被迎戰、甚至進入青年之身，終被送回界外。此戲非故事而是儀器：維持『村之護佑止於何處、黎雅克荒野始於何處』之邊界。功能：以戲維持村界對抗黎雅克世界、以身體記憶傳承加隆·阿朗傳說、在祭司監督下安全地管理附體（刺胸高潮）、並平衡村社兩面——巴龍之護與蘭達之險——兩者皆必需、皆為村所有、皆留在廟垣之內。

functions: Maintains the village boundary against the leyak world
Transmits the Calon Arang legend as embodied community memory
Manages trance-possession safely inside ritual, under priestly supervision
Balances protection and menace as both owned by the village

passages.text: The barong, the shaggy lion-dragon kept in the temple shed as a village treasure, dances against Rangda the widow-witch — fangs, pendulous breasts and the mane of white hair — whose leyak followers swarm behind her. The kris dancers of the village dance between the two powers; at the climax Rangda's power enters them and they turn the daggers on their own breasts in trance — the blades bending, unable to pierce — until incense breaks the trance and the dancers are led back to themselves. The play does not end in victory: Rangda retreats toward the graveyard, the barong stands between, and the village has tested its boundary — the destructive force met, entered, and returned outside the line where the community's protection stops.

title.en: The Leyak: Headless Fliers of the Balinese Night
title.zh: 黎雅克：巴釐夜間的無首飛者

region.zh: 巴釐的十字路口與墳場

summary.en: The leyak are the night-witches of Bali: men and women who at night detach their heads from their bodies, trailing their glowing entrails behind them like a fiery organ-light, to fly to graveyards and crossroads and feed on the unborn and the sick. Their queen is Rangda; against them hang the offerings and paper squares at every door, and the effigies that catch them at the crossroads.
summary.zh: 黎雅克乃巴釐之夜巫：男女於夜間自頸取首，臟腑發光如焰尾曳於身後，飛往墳場十字路口，吸食胎兒與病者之精氣。其後即蘭達；家家門前懸紙方與供品、路口立草人相迎相捕，皆為防黎雅克而設。

sensitivity.note: Living folklore; avoid applying witch-labels to any living person or community.

passages.text: The leyak of Balinese night-lore are humans who at night leave their bodies: the head flies with the glowing entrails trailing behind, to the graveyards and crossroads where the dead are fed, and to the houses of the sick and pregnant. Against them hang the small offerings and paper squares at every doorway, and the effigies set at the crossroads; Rangda is their queen, and the Barong-Rangda drama of the temple festival is the village's regular answer to their kind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Balinese leyak cycle; not verbatim.

title.en: The Ramayana in Bali: Sita's Abduction and the Monkey Chorus
title.zh: 巴釐的《羅摩衍那》：悉多被劫與群猴合唱

texts.period: Balinese Ramayana tradition (Phalgunadi's Balinese Ramayana editions, 1990s, on older village cycles); kecak form c. 1930s

source.work: The Balinese Ramayana cycle (kecak and sendratari forms; I Gusti Putu Phalgunadi, The Balinese Ramayana)

texts.license: Living tradition; paraphrase of copyrighted editions not permitted — narrative summarized

summary.en: Bali keeps the Ramayana as its own: the island's retellings give Sita's abduction, the burning of Alengka and Rawana's fall in Balinese names and Balinese metres, while the kecak — a sitting chorus of dozens of men chanting 'cak-cak-cak' — carries the war of the monkeys around the fire, Rangda and the barong breaking in at the edges as the play's spirits.
summary.zh: 巴釐視《羅摩衍那》為己有：島上之轉述以巴釐名與巴釐格律講述悉多被劫、焚阿楞迦與十首王之亡；而『克恰克』——數十男子圍火坐唱『恰恰恰』之合唱——載起群猴之戰，蘭達與巴龍則於劇之邊緣現身，作為其靈。

sensitivity.note: Living performance tradition; Phalgunadi's editions are copyrighted — narrative summarized, never quoted.

passages.text: The Balinese retellings of the Ramayana keep the whole arc — the golden deer, the abduction, Hanuman's burning of Alengka, Rawana's fall and Sita's ordeal — in Balinese idiom, with the island's own names for Rama's party and the rakshasa court.
passages.note: Summary of the Balinese Ramayana tradition (cf. Phalgunadi's Balinese Ramayana editions); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the kecak form the war of the monkeys is carried by a seated chorus of chanting men around fire and torchlight; the abduction is danced at the centre, and the drama closes with the entry of Rangda and the barong, the island's own spirits claiming the Ramayana stage as theirs.
passages.note: Summary of the kecak performance tradition; not verbatim.

texts.period: Timorese oral legend; recorded in twentieth-century collections

source.work: The legend of the crocodile and the boy (Timor island-origin legend)

summary.en: A crocodile, stranded far from the sea, is saved by a small boy who carries it back to the water; the grateful reptile promises to repay him, and years later comes for the boy — to carry him not to death but on a last voyage. The crocodile grows old swimming the seas, and when it dies its body becomes the island of Timor, shaped like a crocodile in the map; the Timorese, descendants of the boy, still call the crocodile grandfather and observe its taboos.
summary.zh: 一鱷離海擱淺，為一孩童所救，被背返水中；感恩的鱷允諾報答。多年之後，鱷來尋那孩子——不是索命，而是邀他同行最後一程。鱷游遍大海，垂垂老去；死後其身化為帝汶島——地圖上輪廓如鱷。島民（男孩之後裔）至今稱鱷為祖父，守其禁忌。

sensitivity.note: Island-origin legend shared by Timorese communities on both sides of the island.

texts.canonical_translation: Based on the Timorese oral legend; paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The best-known origin legend of Timor tells how the island itself is a relative.

BEGINNING: THE RESCUE. A crocodile, caught far from the sea on dry land, is found by a small boy; instead of killing it, he carries it on his back to the water and releases it. The crocodile promises to repay the service.

MIDDLE: THE CALL AND THE VOYAGE. Years pass; the crocodile returns — for the boy, now grown, is called by it. It carries him not to death but on a last voyage across the seas, as its guest and friend, and the two travel together as the crocodile grows old.

END: THE ISLAND. When the crocodile dies its vast body stays above the water and hardens into land: the island of Timor, which the map shows shaped like a crocodile, with the mountain ridges for its spines. The boy's descendants are the Timorese, who call the crocodile grandfather, ask its pardon before entering its rivers, and treat the animal as kin rather than vermin.

FUNCTIONS. The legend (1) makes the island a relative, with all the obligations of kinship toward crocodiles; (2) explains the island's shape as a body; (3) polices a shared ecology (the courtesy owed to crocodiles in river and sea); and (4) supplies the comparative island-from-animal motif of the eastern archipelago. The legend's ecology is its point: Timor's rivers and coasts are crocodile country, and the myth converts a lethal neighbour into a relative with a name, a genealogy and an etiquette. Fishermen and river-crossers acknowledge the grandfather crocodile, ask pardon before entering his waters, and distinguish the crocodile that takes a man from the grandfather who would not — a legal distinction inside a kinship. The island's shape seals the reading: on the map Timor's long ridged outline suggests the crocodile floating west to east, the mountain chain for its spines, so that geography confirms genealogy. Eastern-Indonesian parallels — islands from animals, canoes turned to reefs, ancestors as sharks or serpents — surround the Timor tale, but its warmth is distinctive: the island is not a defeated monster but a dying grandfather who carried the boy's line home. The legend also carries the eastern archipelago's oldest register of obligations: the boy's rescue of the stranded crocodile is an act of pity between unequals, and the crocodile's repayment — the last voyage, the island, the descendants — converts a debt between two individuals into a standing covenant between two peoples, the boy's line and the crocodile's. Timorese ritual speech still keeps the terms of that covenant in view: the crocodile is addressed as elder, not hunted as vermin, and the tellings insist that the few crocodiles who break the peace are not the grandfather but his lawless descendants. Read as charter, the myth does what island-origin legends do — it makes the land itself the body of an ancestor — but it does so with the unusual tenderness of a rescue repaid, which is why the tale survives so uniformly on both sides of the island's colonial border.
narrative.zh: 帝汶最著名之由來傳說謂此島本身即親族。開篇：一鱷離海擱於陸地，被孩童發現；男孩不忍殺之，背之返水而釋。鱷允諾報恩。中段：多年後鱷歸來——唤那已成少年的男孩；不是索命，而是邀他作客，同遊最後一程；人與鱷同游四海，鱷漸老。結尾：鱷死，其巨身留於水上硬化為陸——即帝汶島；地圖上其輪廓如鱷，山脊為其棘刺。男孩之後裔即帝汶人，至今稱鱷為祖父，入河下海前先請鱷恕罪，視之為親而非害獸。功能：以親屬關係釋島（對鱷負親族之義）、以屍身釋島形、規訓人鱷共居之生態禮俗、並為東部群島『動物化島』母題供給帝汶之形態。

title.en: The Pasola of Sumba: Riders on the Beach for the Rice-Worms
title.zh: 松巴島帕索拉：騎手為稻蟲而馳

region.zh: 松巴島科迪與瓦努卡卡海岸

source.work: The pasola horse-battle tradition of West Sumba (marapu religion)

summary.en: The pasola of West Sumba opens the planting year: bands of horsemen from rival clans charge each other on the sea-shore with spears — a ritual battle fixed by the date the nyale sea-worms swarm ashore. The blood spilled on the sand is the field's fertilizer and the year's divination: the more it flows, the better the rice; the falling riders read the harvest to come.
summary.zh: 西松巴『帕索拉』開啟耕年：敵對氏族之騎手群於海灘持矛對衝——儀式性戰鬥，其日期由『尼亞勒』海蟲湧岸之日決定。灘上所流之血即田之肥與年之卜：血流愈盛，稻愈豐；墜馬之騎手，即為來年收成之兆。

sensitivity.note: Living ritual battle; note the real risks and the community's own rules.

passages.text: The pasola opens the planting year in West Sumba: horsemen of rival clans charge each other on the sea-shore with spears, the date fixed by the night the nyale sea-worms swarm ashore. The blood spilled on the sand is both fertilizer and oracle — the more it flows, the better the rice; the riders who fall are read as the harvest's signs, and the year's planting proceeds under marapu rules fixed by the battle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Sumba pasola tradition; not verbatim.

source.work: The ngaben cremation rite (Balinese funerary cycle)

summary.en: In Bali the dead are not buried but burned: the ngaben sends the soul's five elements back to their sources — earth to earth, water to water, fire to fire, air to air — through the burning of the sarcophagus and the tower. Raffles' informant noted the Pembakaran, 'the place where the bodies of the princes are burned,' with figures of the deities installed beside it; the ashes go to the river, and the soul, element by element, goes home.
summary.zh: 巴釐亡者不入土而以火歸：『恩加本』將魂之五元素送還其源——土歸土、水歸水、火歸火、風歸風——藉棺槨與塔樓之焚化完成。拉弗爾斯之報告人亦記『彭巴卡蘭』——焚燒王族遺體之地，其旁立有諸神之像；骨灰入河，魂則元素逐一歸家。

passages.text: The ngaben returns the dead by fire: the burning of the sarcophagus and the tower sends the soul's elements back to their sources — earth to earth, water to water, fire to fire, air to air — and the ashes are carried to the river. Raffles' informant records the Pembakaran, the place where the bodies of the princes are burned, with figures of the different deities installed in places made for their reception — the cremation ground itself a temple of the return.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Balinese ngaben tradition; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), Appendix; not verbatim.
